items.followUp: Calculate the number of moles in 9 g of water.

rubric.why: Award for correctly applying the mole relationship to the mass and molar mass of water.
rubric.description: Uses the mass-to-moles relationship and the molar mass of water.
rubric.how: Look for n = m/M, or an equivalent calculation using 6 g and 18 g mol⁻¹ (or their SI equivalents). Accept a correct answer of one-third mole even if the working is omitted here; award the other mark for the final answer separately only if it is clearly stated as the result.

rubric.why: The question asks for the amount of water in moles.
rubric.description: Gives the number of moles with the correct unit.
rubric.how: Check that the result is approximately 0.333 mol.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 6 g = 0.006 kg; molar mass of H₂O, M = 18 g mol⁻¹ = 0.018 kg mol⁻¹

items.followUp: Describe how shielding effect changes down a group and across a period.

rubric.why: More inner electron shells are present farther down a group, increasing shielding.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect increases down a group.
rubric.how: Look for both the direction down a group and an increase in shielding effect.

rubric.why: Across a period, added electrons enter the same principal shell, so shielding changes little.
rubric.description: States that shielding effect remains nearly constant across a period.
rubric.how: Accept 'almost constant' or 'approximately the same' across a period.

modelAnswer: Down a group, the shielding effect increases because the number of inner electron shells increases.
Across a period, the shielding effect remains almost constant because electrons are added to the same shell.

items.followUp: Why are the elements of groups 13 and 14 called p-block elements?

rubric.why: Identifies the groups referred to and their block classification.
rubric.description: Identifies group 1 and group 2 elements as s-block elements.
rubric.how: Look for both groups 1 and 2 and the term s-block.

rubric.why: The block of an element is determined by the subshell into which its last electron enters.
rubric.description: Explains that the differentiating (last) electron enters an s subshell.
rubric.how: Accept equivalent wording that the last or valence electron occupies an s orbital/subshell.

modelAnswer: Elements of groups 1 and 2 are called s-block elements because their last (differentiating) electron enters the s subshell.

items.followUp: Write two properties of polar covalent compounds.

rubric.why: Non-polar covalent compounds generally have weak intermolecular forces and therefore low melting and boiling points.
rubric.description: Gives a correct low melting-point or boiling-point property.
rubric.how: Award for stating either low melting point or low boiling point.

rubric.why: These are characteristic properties of non-polar covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Gives another correct property, such as insolubility in water, solubility in organic solvents, or poor electrical conductivity.
rubric.how: Award for one valid property distinct from the melting/boiling point property.

modelAnswer: Non-polar covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are usually insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, and they do not conduct electricity.

items.followUp: Define a double covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: Defines a single covalent bond as one shared pair of electrons between two atoms.
rubric.how: Look for one pair of electrons shared between atoms.

rubric.why: A valid example completes the requested definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as H₂ or Cl₂.
rubric.how: Accept a molecule with a single covalent bond, including H₂ or Cl₂.

modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.

items.followUp: Show the covalent bond and intermolecular attraction between two HF molecules.

rubric.why: The atoms within an HCl molecule are held together by a polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: Shows or identifies the polar covalent H—Cl bond within a molecule.
rubric.how: Look for H—Cl and its identification as a covalent (polar covalent) bond.

rubric.why: The partial charges on neighbouring HCl molecules attract each other.
rubric.description: Shows or identifies intermolecular attraction between the Cl end of one molecule and the H end of another.
rubric.how: Accept a dipole–dipole attraction or a diagram/description showing Clδ− attracted to Hδ+ of a neighbouring molecule.

modelAnswer: Within an HCl molecule, H and Cl are joined by a polar covalent bond: Hδ+—Clδ−.
Between molecules, the Clδ− end of one molecule attracts the Hδ+ end of another: Hδ+—Clδ− ⋯ Hδ+—Clδ−.
The solid line represents the covalent bond; the dotted line represents the intermolecular dipole–dipole attraction.

items.followUp: Define allotropy and state one reason why an element shows allotropy.

rubric.why: Allotropy describes the occurrence of an element in multiple forms in the same physical state.
rubric.description: Defines allotropy as an element existing in two or more forms in the same physical state.
rubric.how: Look for one element, multiple forms, and the same physical state.

rubric.why: Different atomic or molecular arrangements can give rise to different forms of the same element.
rubric.description: States one reason for allotropy, such as a different arrangement of atoms or a different number of atoms in molecules.
rubric.how: Accept a clear structural or molecular reason for the element having different forms.

modelAnswer: Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different forms in the same physical state.
One reason is that the atoms may be arranged differently in the different forms.

items.followUp: What is the transition temperature of sulfur, and which forms change into each other at this temperature?

rubric.why: Transition temperature is defined by the change from one allotropic form to another.
rubric.description: Defines transition temperature as the temperature at which one allotrope changes into another.
rubric.how: Look for a temperature and a change between allotropic forms.

rubric.why: Sulfur changes from rhombic to monoclinic sulfur at about 95.5 °C.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of the transition temperature of sulfur.
rubric.how: Accept approximately 95.5 °C and the change from rhombic to monoclinic sulfur.

modelAnswer: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotrope changes into another allotrope.
For sulfur, the transition temperature is about 95.5 °C, at which rhombic sulfur changes into monoclinic sulfur.
